title: Culpable homicide vs murder — IPC Sections 299/300 and Exceptions (landmark note)
question: What is the distinction between culpable homicide and murder? Explain Sections 299 and 300 IPC; grave and sudden provocation; State of A.P. v. Rayavarapu Punnayya; Reg v Govinda
content:
QUICK REFERENCE: Section 299 defines culpable homicide. Section 300 makes it murder ONLY under four clauses — (1) intention to cause death, (2) bodily injury known to be likely to cause death, (3) bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, (4) imminently dangerous act — AND only when NONE of the five Exceptions applies. THE FIVE EXCEPTIONS: Exception 1 is grave and sudden provocation; Exception 2 is exceeding private defence in good faith without premeditation; Exception 3 is a public servant exceeding legal powers in good faith; Exception 4 is sudden fight in heat of passion without premeditation and without cruelty or undue advantage; Exception 5 is consent of a deceased person above 18 taking the risk.

DISTINCTION BETWEEN CULPABLE HOMICIDE (SECTION 299 IPC) AND MURDER (SECTION 300 IPC)

Section 299 defines culpable homicide generally: causing death by doing an act with (a) the intention of causing death, or (b) the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or (c) the knowledge that the act is likely to cause death.

Section 300 provides that culpable homicide IS murder when the act falls under any of four clauses: Firstly — intention to cause death; Secondly — intention to cause such bodily injury as the offender knows to be likely to cause death; Thirdly — intention to cause bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; Fourthly — knowledge that the act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death, committed without excuse.

In short: every murder is culpable homicide, but culpable homicide is murder only when it meets one of Section 300's four clauses AND none of its five Exceptions applies.

THE FIVE EXCEPTIONS TO SECTION 300 (culpable homicide NOT amounting to murder): Exception 1 — grave and sudden provocation depriving self-control (provocation must not be sought, voluntary, or by lawful act); Exception 2 — exceeding the right of private defence, in good faith, without premeditation; Exception 3 — a public servant exceeding powers given by law, in good faith; Exception 4 — sudden fight in the heat of passion, without premeditation and without undue advantage or cruelty; Exception 5 — death caused with the consent of the deceased person above 18 years who takes the risk.

State of A.P. v. Rayavarapu Punnayya (AIR 1977 SC 45) lays down the three practical degrees: (1) intention to cause death — punishable as murder under Section 302; (2) intention to cause bodily injury likely to cause death — culpable homicide punishable under the First Part of Section 304; (3) mere knowledge that the act is likely to cause death, without intention — punishable under the Second Part of Section 304.

Reg v. Govinda (1876 ILR 1 Bom 342) illustrates intention versus knowledge: one who administers poison intending death commits murder; one who knows the dose is risky but acts without that intent commits culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

Punishments: murder — Section 302 (death or life imprisonment with fine); culpable homicide not amounting to murder — Section 304 (Part I: life or up to 10 years; Part II: up to 10 years, or fine, or both).

Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Section 100 corresponds to Section 299 (culpable homicide), Section 101 to Section 300 (murder), Section 103 punishes murder, and Section 105 punishes culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The five exceptions are retained in substance.

title: IPC to BNS correspondence — key homicide and bail provisions (landmark note)
question: What is the BNS equivalent of IPC Sections 299 300 302 304? BNS correspondence murder culpable homicide; BNSS anticipatory bail default bail sections
content:
KEY IPC/CRPC TO BNS/BNSS CORRESPONDENCE (criminal law)

Culpable homicide defined: IPC Section 299 corresponds to BNS Section 100. Murder defined: IPC Section 300 corresponds to BNS Section 101. Punishment for murder: IPC Section 302 corresponds to BNS Section 103. Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder: IPC Section 304 corresponds to BNS Section 105. Attempt to murder: IPC Section 307 corresponds to BNS Section 109. Causing death by negligence: IPC Section 304A corresponds to BNS Section 106.

Remand and default bail: CrPC Section 167 corresponds to BNSS Section 187 — police custody up to 15 days, then judicial custody; failure to file the chargesheet within 60 days (offences punishable up to 10 years) or 90 days (offences punishable with death, life, or 10+ years) gives the accused the indefeasible right to default bail.

Anticipatory bail: CrPC Section 438 corresponds to BNSS Section 482. Regular bail provisions CrPC Sections 437/439 correspond broadly to BNSS Sections 480/483.

Note: the new codes apply to offences and proceedings arising after 1 July 2024; cases under investigation or trial under the old codes generally continue under them (saving provisions). Always verify which code governs the facts in question.

title: Basic Structure doctrine — Kesavananda to Minerva Mills (landmark note)
question: What is the Basic Structure doctrine? Kesavananda Bharati Minerva Mills Waman Rao; limits on Parliament's amending power Article 368
content:
THE BASIC STRUCTURE DOCTRINE

Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (AIR 1973 SC 1461), decided 24 April 1973 by a 13-judge bench with a 7:6 majority, holds that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is limited: it cannot alter or destroy the basic structure of the Constitution, even by constitutional amendment.

The Court did not exhaustively define basic structure, but illustrative features include: supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, separation of powers, judicial review, free and fair elections, federalism, secularism, unity and integrity of the nation, and the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

Minerva Mills v. Union of India (AIR 1980 SC 1789) struck down clauses of Article 368 (inserted by the 42nd Amendment) that barred judicial review of amendments, holding that limited amending power is itself part of the basic structure, and that harmony between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is essential.

Waman Rao v. Union of India (AIR 1981 SC 271) applied the doctrine prospectively: Ninth Schedule insertions after 24 April 1973 are open to challenge on basic-structure grounds.

Crucial nuance examiners and practitioners get wrong: Parliament CAN amend any provision including Fundamental Rights — Kesavananda overruled Golaknath v. State of Punjab (AIR 1967 SC 1643), which had barred FR amendments entirely. The ONLY limit is that no amendment may alter or destroy the basic structure. Never state that fundamental rights cannot be amended.

title: Article 21 right to life — Maneka Gandhi to Puttaswamy (landmark note)
question: What is Article 21 right to life and personal liberty? Maneka Gandhi procedure established by law; Puttaswamy privacy; Olga Tellis livelihood
content:
ARTICLE 21 — PROTECTION OF LIFE AND PERSONAL LIBERTY

Article 21 provides that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (AIR 1978 SC 597) transformed the provision: overruling the narrow reading in A.K. Gopalan, the Court held that 'procedure established by law' must be fair, just and reasonable — not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive. The procedure must also satisfy Articles 14 and 19.

Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (AIR 1986 SC 180) held that the right to livelihood is part of the right to life, since no one can live without the means of living.

Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (decided 24 August 2017, 9-judge bench) unanimously held that the right to privacy is intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21, overruling M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh on that point. Subsequent expansion covers dignity, speedy trial, legal aid, shelter, health, and a clean environment.

title: Anticipatory bail Section 438 CrPC — Sibbia to Sushila Aggarwal (landmark note)
question: When can anticipatory bail be granted under Section 438 CrPC? Sushila Aggarwal time limit; Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia; Siddharam Mhetre factors; BNSS 482
content:
ANTICIPATORY BAIL UNDER SECTION 438 CRPC (NOW BNSS SECTION 482)

Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab (AIR 1980 SC 1632), a five-judge Constitution Bench, is the foundation: the power to grant anticipatory bail is discretionary and extraordinary, to be exercised sparingly in exceptional circumstances, considering the nature and gravity of the accusation, the applicant's antecedents, and the possibility of fleeing justice or tampering with witnesses.

Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre v. State of Maharashtra (AIR 2011 SC 312) laid down guiding factors courts must weigh, stressing that frivolous accusations and humiliation by arrest deserve protection while serious economic offences and societal harm weigh against it.

Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi) (AIR 2020 SC 221), a five-judge bench, settled two points: (1) anticipatory bail need NOT be limited to a fixed time period — protection ordinarily continues till the end of trial, though courts may impose conditions or limit duration in appropriate cases; (2) no extraordinary or exceptional threshold beyond the statute is required as a routine rule.

Anticipatory bail applies to non-bailable offences on apprehension of arrest; it cannot be sought after arrest (regular bail then applies). Under the BNSS, 2023, the corresponding provision is Section 482.

title: Default bail Section 167(2) CrPC — 60/90 days and indefeasible right (landmark note)
question: What is default bail under Section 167 CrPC? 60 90 days chargesheet; indefeasible right; Rakesh Kumar Paul; M Ravindran; BNSS 187
content:
DEFAULT (STATUTORY) BAIL UNDER SECTION 167(2) CRPC (NOW BNSS SECTION 187)

When investigation is not completed within the statutory period, the accused acquires an indefeasible right to bail: 60 days where the offence is punishable with imprisonment up to 10 years, and 90 days where punishable with death, life imprisonment, or 10 years and above. Police custody cannot exceed 15 days in the first phase; the remainder is judicial custody.

Rakesh Kumar Paul v. State of Assam (AIR 2017 SC 394) holds the right accrues on expiry of the period and must be availed before the chargesheet is filed — once the chargesheet is filed, the indefeasible right is extinguished.

M. Ravindran v. Intelligence Officer, Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (2021) clarifies the accused need only apply for default bail and show willingness to furnish bail; courts cannot defeat the right on technicalities, and the right survives if the application precedes the filing of the chargesheet.

Under the BNSS, 2023, the corresponding provision is Section 187, retaining the 60/90-day structure.

title: Maintenance Section 125 CrPC — who can claim and how quantum is fixed (landmark note)
question: Who can claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC? maintenance wife children parents quantum how decided; BNSS 144
content: QUICK REFERENCE: Section 125 CrPC (now Section 144 BNSS, 2023) is a summary, social-justice remedy against vagrancy — not a final determination of civil rights. FOUR classes can claim: (1) wife, including a divorced wife who has not remarried, if she is unable to maintain herself; (2) legitimate or illegitimate minor child, whether married or not, unable to maintain itself; (3) legitimate or illegitimate child (not being married daughter) who has attained majority but is unable to maintain itself by reason of physical or mental abnormality or injury; (4) father or mother unable to maintain themselves. A wife living separately by mutual consent, or living in adultery, or refusing without sufficient reason to live with her husband, is disentitled. QUANTUM: since the 2001 amendment there is NO statutory monthly ceiling; the Magistrate of the First Class fixes a monthly allowance based on the means and needs of the parties — the husband's income and status, the wife's reasonable needs, number of dependents. Interim maintenance can be granted during proceedings. Wilful non-compliance is enforceable by warrant and up to one month's imprisonment per defaulted month. Key cases: Shah Bano (AIR 1985 SC 945) on divorced Muslim women's rights (led to the 1986 Act); Danial Latifi (2001) upholding reasonable and fair provision; Bhuwan Mohan Singh v. Meena (2015) 6 SCC 397 on timely payment and quantum.

title: Oppression and mismanagement Companies Act Sections 241-242 (landmark note)
question: What is oppression and mismanagement under the Companies Act? Sections 241 242 NCLT; Foss v Harbottle exception
content: QUICK REFERENCE: Sections 241–242 of the Companies Act, 2013 provide the remedy against oppression and mismanagement — the principal exception to the rule in Foss v. Harbottle (majority rule). WHO MAY APPLY (Section 244): in a company with share capital — at least 100 members or 1/10th of total members (whichever is less), or members holding at least 1/10th of issued share capital; the Tribunal may waive these thresholds. OPPRESSION (Section 241(1)(a)): affairs conducted in a manner prejudicial or oppressive to any member(s), or prejudicial to public interest, or to the company's interests. MISMANAGEMENT (Section 241(1)(b)): any material change in management or control — by alteration of board, share transfers, or otherwise — likely to prejudice members or the company. POWERS OF THE TRIBUNAL (Section 242): regulate future conduct of affairs; purchase of shares by the company or other members; termination or modification of agreements with directors/managers; setting aside transfers; recovery of undue gains; appointing directors; imposing costs. NCLT is the forum; appeal lies to NCLAT then the Supreme Court.

title: Motor accident compensation — hit-and-run, no-fault, Solatium Fund (landmark note)
question: What compensation is available for hit-and-run accident victims? Motor Vehicles Act Sections 140 161 163A 164 solatium fund; no-fault liability
content: QUICK REFERENCE: Motor Vehicles Act compensation routes. (1) FAULT-BASED (Section 166, now 166 MV Act): claim before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal proving rash/negligent driving; compensation for loss of dependency, consortium, funeral expenses. (2) NO-FAULT (Section 140, now Section 164(1) MV Act as amended 2019): fixed-sum liability without proving fault — historically Rs.50,000 for death and Rs.25,000 for permanent disablement. (3) STRUCTURED FORMULA (Section 163A, now Section 163A retained): Second Schedule multiplier compensation without proving negligence, for victims within the income ceiling. (4) HIT-AND-RUN (Section 161, now Sections 164/164A/164B after the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019): special provisions where the offending vehicle is untraced — compensation from the Solatium Fund; the 2019 amendments raised hit-and-run compensation to Rs.2 lakh for death and Rs.50,000 for grievous hurt. Always verify current figures — 2019 amendments substantially revised amounts and added the Motor Vehicle Accident Fund (Section 164B). Key cases: National Insurance v. Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680 (multiplier, future prospects, conventional heads); Sarla Verma v. DTC (2009) 6 SCC 121 (multiplier table).

title: Adverse possession and limitation — Article 65, 12 years private 30 years government (landmark note)
question: What is the limitation period for adverse possession? Article 65 Limitation Act 12 years 30 years government; animus possidendi
content: QUICK REFERENCE: Adverse possession in India is governed by Article 65 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963 (suits for possession of immovable property based on title): TWELVE YEARS from when possession becomes adverse to the plaintiff — THIRTY YEARS where the property belongs to the State/Central Government. There is NO 1996 amendment changing this to six years; any such claim is incorrect. Essentials the possessor must prove: continuous, open, uninterrupted, hostile possession (nec vi, nec clam, nec precario) with animus possidendi (intention to hold as owner) for the full period. Mere long possession is not enough. Section 27 extinguishes the true owner's title on expiry of the period. Mere permissive occupation (tenant, licensee, caretaker) can never mature into adverse possession. Key cases: Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India (2004) 10 SCC 779 (ingredients restated); T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa (2006) 7 SCC 570 (hostile intent must be proved); Ravinder Kaur Grewal v. Manjit Kaur (2019) 8 SCC 729 (adverse possessor can also sue for declaration of title).

title: Consumer Protection Act 2019 — commissions, jurisdiction, reliefs (landmark note)
question: What reliefs can consumer commissions grant? Consumer Protection Act 2019 District State National Commission pecuniary jurisdiction limits
content: QUICK REFERENCE — CONSUMER PROTECTION ACT, 2019 (replaced the 1986 Act; do NOT state 1986 forum names or limits as current law). Three-tier quasi-judicial machinery, now called COMMISSIONS (not Forums): District Commission, State Commission, National Commission. PECUNIARY JURISDICTION (as revised by the 2021 Rules): District — claims up to Rs.50 lakh; State — above Rs.50 lakh up to Rs.2 crore; National — above Rs.2 crore. (The 1986 Act's District Forum/State Commission/National Commission with Rs.20 lakh/Rs.1 crore limits are REPEALED — never cite them.) RELIEFS (Section 39): removal of defects/deficiencies; replacement of goods; refund of price; compensation for loss or injury including mental agony; punitive damages; discontinuance of unfair trade practices; withdrawal of hazardous goods; costs of litigation. E-commerce and misleading advertisements are expressly covered (Central Consumer Protection Authority). Appeal: District to State (45 days), State to National (30 days), National to Supreme Court (30 days). Key cases: Rajeev Hitendra Pathak v. Achyut Kashinath Karekar (2011) 9 SCC 541 (commissions have no review power — under the 1986 Act, position substantially retained); Experion Developers v. Sushma Shiroor (2022) on delayed possession relief.
